questions.question: ______ is a pile in which items are added at one end and removed from the other.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) Queue**

- **Opposite-End FIFO Access:** A **queue** inserts items at one end (**`rear`**) and removes them from the opposite end (**`front`**), enforcing **First-In-First-Out (FIFO)** order.
- **Contrast:** A **stack** (`C`) adds and removes at the *same* end (`top`), while lists/arrays (`A`, `D`) permit arbitrary index/node access.

questions.question: Which of the following is non-linear data structure?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Trees**

- **Hierarchical `1 : Many` Branching:** A **tree** organizes nodes across parent-child levels where one node may branch to multiple children, making it a **non-linear** data structure.
- **Why Others Are Linear:** Both **Stacks** (`B`) and **Strings** (`C`, character arrays) store elements in a sequential `1 : 1` chain.

questions.question: ______ is not the operation that can be performed on queue.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Traversal**

- **Restricted End-Only ADT:** A strict **Queue ADT** exposes only **`Insertion` (`enqueue` at `rear`)**, **`Deletion` (`dequeue` from `front`)**, and **`Retrieval` (`peek` at `front`)** (plus `isEmpty`/`isFull`).
- **Why Not Traversal:** Visiting interior elements sequentially (**traversal**) violates queue encapsulation, which hides elements between `front` and `rear`.

questions.question: Which is/are the application(s) of stack?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) All of the above**

- **Core Stack Applications:**
  - **Function Calls (`A`):** Stores return addresses, parameters, and local activation frames.
  - **Large-Number Arithmetic (`B`):** Pushes digits most-significant-first so least-significant digits pop first for carry propagation.
  - **Arithmetic Expressions (`C`):** Powers infix-to-postfix/prefix conversion and RPN evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following data structures are indexed structures?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) Linear arrays**

- **Direct Subscript Indexing:** **Linear arrays** store homogeneous elements contiguously so any element `A[i]` is addressed directly by its integer **index** in `O(1)` time (`Base + (i - LB) * w`).
- **Why Others Differ:** **Stacks** (`A`) expose only `top`, and **Linked lists** (`B`) require `O(n)` pointer traversal.

questions.question: Linear arrays are also called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) One-dimensional array**

- **Single-Subscript Sequence:** A **linear array** requires exactly **one subscript** `A[i]` (`LB <= i <= UB`) to identify any element along a single logical dimension, so it is synonymously called a **one-dimensional (`1D`) array** (unlike `2D` row-column matrices).

questions.question: Binary trees with threads are called as ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) Threaded trees**

- **Repurposing `NULL` Child Pointers:** An `n`-node binary tree has `n + 1` wasted `NULL` child pointers; replacing them with special **threads** pointing to each node's **in-order predecessor and/or successor** creates a **threaded binary tree**, enabling stack-free, recursion-free `O(n)` in-order traversal.

questions.question: In Binary trees nodes with no successor are called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) Terminal nodes**

- **Zero Out-Degree (`Leaf`):** In standard Lipschutz/Seymour tree terminology, binary-tree nodes having **no successors (zero children, `left == NULL` and `right == NULL`)** are formally called **terminal nodes** (or **leaf / external nodes**), as opposed to *non-terminal (internal)* nodes.

questions.question: The depth `Dn` of a complete binary tree of n nodes is given by ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) `Dn = log₂ n`**

- **Logarithmic Complete-Tree Depth:** Because a complete binary tree fills every level before starting the next (`2^d <= n < 2^(d + 1)`), its edge depth is `Dn = floor(log₂ n)` (or `floor(log₂ n) + 1` levels in Lipschutz), growing as **`log₂ n`**.
questions.sourceNote: The scan flattens exponents; C is restored as `log₂ n`.

questions.question: Every node N in a binary tree T except the root has a unique parent called the ______ of N.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Predecessor**

- **Immediate Upward Link:** In Lipschutz's verbatim definition of a binary tree `T`, every node `N` except the root has a unique parent node called the **(immediate) predecessor** of `N`, while `N`'s children are its immediate *successors*.

questions.question: The in-order traversal of tree will yield a sorted listing of elements of tree in ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) Binary search trees**

- **BST Ordering Invariant:** Every node in a **Binary Search Tree (BST)** satisfies `all keys(left) < key(node) < all keys(right)`, so **in-order traversal (`Left -> Root -> Right`)** visits keys in strictly **sorted ascending order** (unlike an arbitrary binary tree `C`; AVL `B` inherits this because it is a balanced BST).

questions.question: The post-order traversal of a binary tree is `DEBFCA`. Find out the pre-order traversal.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) `ABDECF`**

- **Root & Standard Companion Split:** The last token of post-order `DEBFCA` fixes the **root = `A`** (`Pre` starts with `A`). Paired with the standard textbook companion in-order `DBEAFC`, left subtree `(In: DBE, Post: DEB)` has root `B` (`D, E`), and right subtree `(In: FC, Post: FC)` has root `C` (left `F`) -> Pre-order **`ABDECF`**.
questions.sourceNote: Postorder alone cannot uniquely determine a tree; C is the model answer when paired with inorder `DBEAFC`, the same sequence pair used in the December 2024 paper.

questions.question: Three standards ways of traversing a binary tree T with root R ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) Pre-order, in-order, post-order**

- **Three Standard Depth-First Tree Traversals:**
  - **Pre-order:** `Root -> Left -> Right`
  - **In-order:** `Left -> Root -> Right`
  - **Post-order:** `Left -> Right -> Root`
  *(Note: `Prefix, infix, postfix` in `A` name algebraic expression notations, not tree traversal algorithms.)*

questions.question: A full binary tree with n leaves contains ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) `2n − 1` nodes**

- **Full (Strict) Binary Tree Identity:** Every non-leaf node in a full binary tree has **degree `2`** (`n₁ = 0`). Applying `n₀ = n₂ + 1` with `n₀ = n` leaves gives `n₂ = n - 1` internal nodes, so total nodes `N = n₀ + n₂ = n + (n - 1) =` **`2n - 1`**.

questions.question: The smallest element of an array’s index is called its ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) lower bound**

- **Index Bounds Terminology:** For an array `A[LB .. UB]`, the **smallest valid subscript `LB`** is its **lower bound** (`0` in C), the largest valid subscript `UB` is its **upper bound** (`D`), and the array length is `UB - LB + 1`.

questions.question: The data structure required for Breadth First Search on a graph is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) queue**

- **Level-Order Wavefront:** **Breadth-First Search (BFS)** explores all vertices at distance `k` from the source before advancing to distance `k + 1`, using a **FIFO queue** to hold discovered-but-unexpanded frontier vertices (whereas **DFS** uses a **stack** `B`).

questions.question: The data structure required to evaluate a postfix expression is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) stack**

- **LIFO Operand Pairing:** Scanning a postfix expression left to right pushes operands onto a **stack**; whenever an operator arrives, the **two most recently pushed operands** pop off the top (`B = pop()`, `A = pop()`), evaluate `A op B`, and push the result back.

questions.question: The postfix form of `A*B + C/D` is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) `AB*CD/+`**

- **Precedence Step-by-Step:** Multiplication `*` and division `/` bind tighter than `+`: `(A * B)` converts to `A B *`, `(C / D)` converts to `C D /`, and joining both sub-expressions with `+` yields **`AB*CD/+`**.
questions.sourceNote: OCR corrupted the infix expression to `A*l+C/D`; restored as `A*B + C/D` from the page image.

questions.question: A linear collection of data elements where the next node is given by means of pointer is called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Linked list**

- **Pointer-Chained Sequence:** A **linked list** stores a linear sequence of dynamically allocated nodes in non-contiguous heap memory where each node explicitly holds data plus a **pointer (`next`)** giving the address of the following node.

questions.question: Representation of data structure in memory is known as ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Storage structure**

- **Main-Memory Realization:** The concrete physical representation of a logical data model inside **main memory (RAM)**—such as sequential arrays or linked heap nodes—is called a **storage structure** (whereas representation on secondary disk is a *file structure* `B`, and the logical interface is an *ADT* `C`).

questions.question: For an undirected graph with n vertices and e edges, the sum of the degree of each vertex is equal to ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) `2e`**

- **Handshaking Lemma:** Every undirected edge `(u, v)` has two endpoints and therefore contributes `+1` to `deg(u)` and `+1` to `deg(v)` (`+2` for a self-loop). Summing `deg(v)` across all `n` vertices counts every one of the `e` edges twice, yielding **`2e`**.

questions.question: Which of the following data structure is nonlinear type?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Graph**

- **Many-to-Many Network:** A **graph** `G = (V, E)` connects any vertex to zero, one, or many arbitrary neighbours (including cycles), making it **non-linear**, whereas **Stacks** (`B`) and **Lists** (`C`) arrange items in a linear `1 : 1` sequence.

questions.question: When new data are to be inserted into a data structure, but there is no available space; this situation is usually called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Overflow**

- **Full-Capacity Insertion Error:** Attempting to insert a new item when a bounded array (`TOP == MAX - 1`) or free-storage pool (`AVAIL == NULL`) has **no remaining space** raises an **Overflow** condition (whereas deleting from an empty structure raises **Underflow** `B`).

questions.question: A data structure where elements can be added or removed at either end but not in the middle is called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) dequeue**

- **Double-Ended Queue (`Deque`):** A **deque** (often spelled *dequeue* in university papers) permits **`O(1)` insertion and deletion at both the `front` and `rear` ends** while forbidding middle access—generalizing both stacks (`A`) and ordinary FIFO queues (`B`).

questions.question: Which of the following is not the type of queue?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) Single ended queue**

- **Standard Queue Taxonomy:** **Ordinary (linear) queue** (`C`), **Circular queue** (`B`), **Priority queue** (`A`), and **Double-ended queue (`Deque`)** are the standard recognized queue variants; *"Single ended queue"* (`D`) is not a valid queue type (a single-ended structure is a **stack**).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 Marks
> **a) Primitive & Non-Primitive DS (`3m`)** | **b) Linear & Non-Linear DS (`3m`)** | **c) Data Type vs Data Structure (`2m`)**.

### a) Primitive and Non-Primitive Data Structures (3 Marks)

- **Primitive Data Structures:** Fundamental atomic scalar values directly supported and manipulated by machine-level CPU instructions.
  - *Examples:* Integer (`int`), Floating-point (`float`, `double`), Character (`char`), Boolean, and Memory Pointer.
- **Non-Primitive Data Structures:** Composite structures synthesized from primitive types to organize multi-element collections and support structured operations (`insert`, `delete`, `search`, `sort`).
  - *Examples:* **Arrays**, **Linked Lists**, **Stacks**, **Queues**, **Trees**, and **Graphs**.

### b) Linear and Non-Linear Data Structures (3 Marks)

- **Linear Data Structure:** Arranges elements sequentially in a `1 : 1` adjacency chain where every interior element has a unique immediate predecessor and successor, enabling single-pass traversal.
  - *Examples:* **Linear Array**, **Linked List**, **Stack**, **Queue**.
- **Non-Linear Data Structure:** Connects one element to multiple elements hierarchically (`1 : many`) or arbitrarily (`many : many`), so elements cannot be visited in a single linear run without branching.
  - *Examples:* **Binary / AVL / B-Trees** and **Graphs**.

### c) Data Type vs Data Structure (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Data Type vs Data Structure
> | Parameter | Data Type | Data Structure |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Focus** | Defines the **domain of values** and legal scalar operations of a variable (`int`, `float`). | Defines the **inter-element organization** and algorithmic operations over a collection. |
> | **Complexity Scope** | Atomic operations execute in `O(1)` hardware cycles. | Operations carry algorithmic time/space trade-offs (`O(1)`, `O(log n)`, `O(n)`). |
> | **Examples** | `int`, `char`, `double`. | Stack, Queue, Linked List, BST, Graph. |

a) Write an algorithm for PUSH and POP operations on STACK using array.
b) Convert the following Infix expression into prefix expression: `(A-D/C) * (D+E-F)`.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Convert the following Infix expression into prefix expression: `(A-D/C) * (D+E-F)`.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks
> **a) Array `PUSH` & `POP` Algorithms (`2m + 2m = 4m`)** | **b) Infix-to-Prefix Conversion of `(A-D/C) * (D+E-F)` (`4m`)** -> **`* - A / D C - + D E F`**.

### a) `PUSH` and `POP` Operations on `STACK` Using an Array (4 Marks)

```text
[STACK[0 .. MAX - 1] is a 1D array; initially TOP = -1]

Algorithm PUSH(STACK, TOP, MAX, ITEM)
1. If TOP == MAX - 1 then
       Write "STACK OVERFLOW" and Return
2. TOP = TOP + 1
3. STACK[TOP] = ITEM
4. Return

Algorithm POP(STACK, TOP)
1. If TOP == -1 then
       Write "STACK UNDERFLOW" and Return
2. ITEM = STACK[TOP]
3. TOP = TOP - 1
4. Return ITEM
```

- **Complexity:** Both operations run in **`O(1)` time** and **`O(1)` extra space**.

### b) Convert Infix `(A - D / C) * (D + E - F)` into Prefix (4 Marks)

- **Method 1 — Reverse-Infix -> Postfix -> Reverse (`3` Steps):**
  1. **Reverse Infix & Swap `(` <-> `)`:**
     `(F - E + D) * (C / D - A)`
  2. **Convert Reversed Expression to Postfix** *(for left-associative `+`/`-`, equal-precedence operators are **not** popped on reversal so original left-to-right grouping `((D + E) - F)` is preserved)*:

| Scanned Token | Operator Stack (`bottom -> top`) | Postfix Output |
|---|---|---|
| `( F - E + D )` | `(` -> `(-` -> `(- +` -> pop `+`, `-` | `F E D + -` |
| `*` | `*` | `F E D + -` |
| `( C / D - A )` | `* (` -> `* ( /` -> pop `/`, push `-` -> pop `-` | `F E D + - C D / A -` |
| End of input | Pop `*` | **`F E D + - C D / A - *`** |

  3. **Reverse the Postfix Result to Obtain Prefix:**
     **`* - A / D C - + D E F`** *(compactly: `*-A/DC-+DEF`)*.

- **Method 2 — Direct Algebraic Verification (`op Left Right`):**
  - Left factor `(A - (D / C))`: `D / C -> / D C`, then `A - (/ D C)` -> **`- A / D C`**.
  - Right factor `((D + E) - F)`: `D + E -> + D E`, then `(+ D E) - F` -> **`- + D E F`**.
  - Multiply both factors with `*`: **`* - A / D C - + D E F`**.

b) What is a DeQueue? Explain its operation with example.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 5 + 3 = 8 Marks
> **a) Circular Queues + Array `INSERT` & `DELETE` Algorithms (`1m + 2m + 2m = 5m`)** | **b) DeQueue (`Deque`) Definition, Operations & Example (`3m`)**.

### a) Circular Queues & Array Insertion/Deletion Algorithms (5 Marks)

- **Definition:** A **circular queue** connects the last index `MAX - 1` of a queue array back to index `0` in a logical ring using modulo-`MAX` arithmetic, reusing front slots freed by earlier deletions and eliminating **false overflow**.

```text
Algorithm CQ_INSERT(CQ, FRONT, REAR, MAX, ITEM)
[Initially FRONT = -1, REAR = -1]
1. If (REAR + 1) % MAX == FRONT then
       Write "CIRCULAR QUEUE OVERFLOW" and Return
2. If FRONT == -1 then          // Queue was empty
       FRONT = 0
       REAR  = 0
   Else
       REAR  = (REAR + 1) % MAX
3. CQ[REAR] = ITEM
4. Return
```

```text
Algorithm CQ_DELETE(CQ, FRONT, REAR, MAX)
1. If FRONT == -1 then
       Write "CIRCULAR QUEUE UNDERFLOW" and Return
2. ITEM = CQ[FRONT]
3. If FRONT == REAR then        // Removing the single remaining item
       FRONT = -1
       REAR  = -1
   Else
       FRONT = (FRONT + 1) % MAX
4. Return ITEM
```

### b) DeQueue (`Double-Ended Queue`) & Operations with Example (3 Marks)

- **Definition:** A **DeQueue (`Deque`)** is a generalized linear queue in which elements can be **inserted and deleted at both ends (`FRONT` and `REAR`)** in `O(1)` time, with two restricted variants: **Input-Restricted Deque** (insert at one end, delete at both) and **Output-Restricted Deque** (insert at both ends, delete at one).
- **Four Core Operations & Worked Example (starting with `[]`):**
  1. `insertRear(10)` -> `[10]`
  2. `insertRear(20)` -> `[10, 20]`
  3. `insertFront(5)` -> `[5, 10, 20]`
  4. `deleteRear()` (removes `20`) -> `[5, 10]`
  5. `deleteFront()` (removes `5`) -> **`[10]`** *(used in sliding-window maxima, palindrome checking, and work-stealing CPU schedulers)*.

b) Write an algorithm to insert a node at the beginning of a single linked list.

subparts.label: b

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks
> **a) (i) Header Linked List (`2m`) + (ii) Circular Linked List (`2m`)** | **b) SLL Insert-at-Beginning Algorithm (`4m`)**.

### a) Definitions with Examples (4 Marks)

- **(i) Header Linked List (`2m`):** A linked list preceded by a permanent special **header (dummy) node** `HEADER` that holds list-level metadata (e.g., node count) and points to the first actual data node. Because `HEADER` is never `NULL`, front insertions/deletions need no special empty-list branch.
  - *Variants:* **Grounded header list** (`last->next == NULL`) and **Circular header list** (`last->next == HEADER`).

```ascii
  HEADER --> [ count=3 | * ] --> [ 10 | * ] --> [ 20 | * ] --> [ 30 | NULL ]
              (dummy header)      (1st node)
```

- **(ii) Circular Linked List (`2m`):** A linked list in which the `next` field of the **last node points back to the first (`HEAD`) node** instead of `NULL`, forming a closed ring so every node is reachable from any starting node (ideal for Round-Robin CPU scheduling).

```ascii
  HEAD --> [ 10 | * ] --> [ 20 | * ] --> [ 30 | * ] --+
              ^                                       |
              +------------- (last->next = HEAD) -----+
```

### b) Algorithm to Insert a Node at the Beginning of a Singly Linked List (4 Marks)

```text
Algorithm SLL_INSERT_BEGIN(HEAD, ITEM)
1. Allocate a new node NEW from heap memory.
2. If NEW == NULL then
       Write "OVERFLOW: Out of Memory" and Return HEAD
3. Set NEW->data = ITEM
4. Set NEW->next = HEAD      // point NEW to current first node (or NULL if empty)
5. Set HEAD = NEW            // advance HEAD to NEW
6. Return HEAD
```

- **Pointer-Order Rule & Complexity:** Step `4` (`NEW->next = HEAD`) must precede Step `5` (`HEAD = NEW`) so the existing chain is not lost; executes in **`O(1)` constant time** and **`O(1)` extra space**.

a) Write algorithm for Breadth First Search (BFS).
b) Give the complexity.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Write algorithm for Breadth First Search (BFS).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 6 + 2 = 8 Marks
> **a) Breadth-First Search (BFS) Algorithm & Worked Queue Trace (`6m`)** | **b) Time & Space Complexity Analysis (`2m`)**.

### a) Breadth-First Search (BFS) Algorithm & Worked Trace (6 Marks)

```text
Algorithm BFS(G, s)
[Input: Graph G = (V, E) and starting vertex s]

1. For each vertex u in V do
       visited[u] = FALSE
2. Create an empty FIFO queue Q
3. visited[s] = TRUE
4. ENQUEUE(Q, s)
5. While Q is not empty do
       u = DEQUEUE(Q)
       Print u
       For each vertex w adjacent to u do
           If visited[w] == FALSE then
               visited[w] = TRUE
               ENQUEUE(Q, w)
6. Return
```

- **Worked Trace on Example Graph (`A-B, A-C, B-D, B-E, C-E`, Source = `A`):**

```ascii
    [A] --- [B] --- [D]
     |       |
    [C] --- [E]
```

| Step | Dequeued `u` | Newly Marked & Enqueued | Queue `Q` (`front -> rear`) | Output So Far |
|:-:|:-:|---|---|---|
| Init | — | `A` | `[ A ]` | — |
| 1 | `A` | `B, C` | `[ B, C ]` | `A` |
| 2 | `B` | `D, E` | `[ C, D, E ]` | `A, B` |
| 3 | `C` | *(none: `A, E` already visited)* | `[ D, E ]` | `A, B, C` |
| 4 | `D` | *(none)* | `[ E ]` | `A, B, C, D` |
| 5 | `E` | *(none)* | `[ ]` *(empty -> stop)* | **`A, B, C, D, E`** |

### b) Time and Space Complexity of BFS (2 Marks)

- **Time Complexity:**
  - **With Adjacency List — `O(V + E)`:** Every reachable vertex is enqueued/dequeued at most once (`O(V)`), and every adjacency list is scanned once (`sum of deg(u) = 2E` -> `O(E)`).
  - **With Adjacency Matrix — `O(V²)`:** Checking neighbours of each of the `V` vertices scans a row of `V` entries.
- **Space Complexity — `O(V)`:** `visited[V]` array uses `O(V)` space and queue `Q` holds at most `V` vertices simultaneously.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks
> **a) Step-by-Step Alphabetical AVL Tree Construction (`4m`)** | **b) Order-`m` B-Tree Definition & When Preferred (`2m + 2m = 4m`)**.

### a) AVL Tree for `{March, May, November, August, April, January, December, July}` (4 Marks)

- **Lexicographical Key Order:** `April < August < December < January < July < March < May < November` (`BF = h_L - h_R` in `{-1, 0, +1}`).
  1. **Insert `March`:** Root `[March (0)]`.
  2. **Insert `May`:** Right of `March` -> `March(-1) -> R: May(0)`.
  3. **Insert `November`:** Right of `May` -> `March` becomes `BF = -2` (**RR imbalance**) -> **Left Rotation at `March`** -> Root **`May(0)`**, `L: March(0)`, `R: November(0)`.
  4. **Insert `August`:** Left of `March` -> balanced (`May(+1)`).
  5. **Insert `April`:** Left of `August` -> `March` becomes `BF = +2` (**LL imbalance**) -> **Right Rotation at `March`** -> `May(+1)` has left child **`August(0)`** (`L: April`, `R: March`) and right `November`.
  6. **Insert `January`:** Goes left of `March` -> `May` becomes `BF = +2` while `August` has `BF = -1` (**LR imbalance at `May`**) -> **Left-Right Double Rotation** (left-rotate `August`, right-rotate `May`) -> New root **`March(0)`**, left `August(0)` (`April`, `January`), right `May(-1)` (`R: November`).
  7. **Insert `December`:** Left of `January` -> all `|BF| <= 1` (no rotation).
  8. **Insert `July`:** Right of `January` -> all `|BF| <= 1` (no rotation).

```ascii
                        [ March (+1) ]
                      /                \
             [ August (-1) ]        [ May (-1) ]
              /          \                 \
        [April (0)]   [January (0)]    [November (0)]
                       /        \
                [December (0)] [July (0)]
```

### b) B-Tree of Order `m` & When It Is Preferred (4 Marks)

- **Definition (`Order m`):** A self-balancing multiway search tree satisfying:
  1. Every node has **at most `m` children** and **`m - 1` sorted keys**.
  2. Every non-root internal node has **at least `ceil(m / 2)` children** (`ceil(m / 2) - 1` keys).
  3. The root has at least `2` children if it is not a leaf.
  4. **All leaf nodes appear at the exact same depth**.
- **When Preferred:** Preferred whenever datasets **exceed main RAM and reside on block-oriented secondary storage (HDD/SSD)**—such as **RDBMS indexes, NoSQL storage engines, and OS file systems (`NTFS`, `ext4`, `Btrfs`)**—because high branching factor (`m = 100`–`1000` per `4 KB` page) keeps tree height `h <= 3`–`4`, minimizing slow disk I/O reads.

a) Write a recursive function to calculate the GCD of two numbers.
b) Write an algorithm to evaluate a postfix expression.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Write an algorithm to evaluate a postfix expression.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks
> **a) Recursive Euclidean `gcd()` Function in C (`4m`)** | **b) Stack-Based Postfix Evaluation Algorithm & Trace (`4m`)**.

### a) Recursive Function to Calculate GCD of Two Numbers (4 Marks)

- **Euclid's Recurrence:** `gcd(a, 0) = a` *(base case)* and `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)` for `b > 0`.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int gcd(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return a;              /* base case */
    }
    return gcd(b, a % b);      /* tail-recursive Euclidean step */
}

int main(void) {
    printf("GCD(48, 18) = %d\n", gcd(48, 18));
    return 0;
}
```

- **Dry Run for `gcd(48, 18)`:** `gcd(48, 18) -> gcd(18, 12) -> gcd(12, 6) -> gcd(6, 0) ->` **`6`** (`O(log(min(a, b)))` time).

### b) Algorithm to Evaluate a Postfix Expression (4 Marks)

```text
Algorithm EVAL_POSTFIX(EXP)
1. Initialize an empty operand stack S
2. Scan tokens of EXP from left to right:
   a) If token is an operand (number):
          PUSH(S, token)
   b) Else if token is a binary operator op (+, -, *, /, ^):
          val2 = POP(S)          // top = right/second operand
          val1 = POP(S)          // next = left/first operand
          res  = val1 op val2
          PUSH(S, res)
3. RESULT = POP(S)
4. Return RESULT
```

- **Worked Trace on `5  1  2  +  4  *  +  3  -`:**
  - Push operands `5, 1, 2` -> Stack `[5, 1, 2]`
  - `+` pops `2` (`val2`) and `1` (`val1`) -> `1 + 2 = 3` -> Stack `[5, 3]`; Push `4` -> `[5, 3, 4]`
  - `*` pops `4` (`val2`) and `3` (`val1`) -> `3 * 4 = 12` -> Stack `[5, 12]`; `+` pops `12, 5` -> `5 + 12 = 17` -> `[17]`
  - Push `3` -> `[17, 3]`; `-` pops `3` (`val2`) and `17` (`val1`) -> `17 - 3 =` **`14`**.
- **Operand-Order Rule & Complexity:** For non-commutative `-`, `/`, and `^`, always compute `val1 op val2` (`second_popped op first_popped`); executes in **`O(n)` linear time** and **`O(n)` stack space**.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks
> **a) Short Notes: (i) ADT (`2m`) + (ii) Threaded Binary Tree (`2m`)** | **b) In-Order, Pre-Order & Post-Order of Printed Tree (`4m`)**.

### a) Short Notes (4 Marks)

- **(i) Abstract Data Type (ADT) (`2m`):** A mathematical model of a data type defined strictly by its **logical value domain** and the **specification of operations** (`push`, `pop`, `enqueue`, `dequeue`) independent of concrete representation or language. Changing a `Stack` ADT's internal representation from a fixed array to a linked list requires zero changes in caller code (**information hiding**).
- **(ii) Threaded Binary Tree (`2m`):** An `n`-node binary tree normally wastes **`n + 1` `NULL` child pointers**. A **threaded binary tree** replaces `NULL` links with special **threads** (`lthread`/`rthread` boolean tags distinguish real children from threads): a `NULL` left link points to the node's **in-order predecessor**, and a `NULL` right link points to its **in-order successor**, enabling **`O(n)` in-order traversal in `O(1)` auxiliary space without recursion or a stack**.

```ascii
  Node Layout: [ ltag | left | data | right | rtag ]  (tag=0: child, tag=1: thread)
```

### b) Traversals of the Printed Binary Tree (4 Marks)

```ascii
                [5]
              /     \
            [7]     [9]
            /      /   \
          [3]    [2]   [4]
         /   \           \
       [1]   [6]         [8]
```

- **In-Order (`Left -> Root -> Right`):**
  `In(7) = 1 3 6 7`, Root = **`5`**, `In(9) = 2 9 4 8` -> **`1  3  6  7  5  2  9  4  8`**
- **Pre-Order (`Root -> Left -> Right`):**
  Root = **`5`**, `Pre(7) = 7 3 1 6`, `Pre(9) = 9 2 4 8` -> **`5  7  3  1  6  9  2  4  8`**
- **Post-Order (`Left -> Right -> Root`):**
  `Post(7) = 1 6 3 7`, `Post(9) = 2 8 4 9`, Root = **`5`** -> **`1  6  3  7  2  8  4  9  5`**
